newsitem.title: INDONESIA: No letter yet from Mandela on Xanana - Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: No letter yet from Mandela on Xanana - Indonesia.

text.p: Indonesia said on Thursday that it had yet to receive a letter from South African President Nelson Mandela urging the release of East Timorese rebel leader Jose "Xanana" Gusmao from jail.

"This afternoon President Suharto asked me whether any letter has arrived from President Mandela," State Secretary Murdiono told reporters at the presidential palace. "What I can say at this moment is that President Suharto has not received that letter."
Mandela said on Wednesday he had urged the release of Gusmao in an initiative to settle a dispute over the troubled territory.

"In the letter I have written to President Suharto I have recommended that Mr Gusmao must be freed," Mandela, once the world's most famous political prisoner, told reporters in Pretoria after a meeting with Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio.
The South African leader said the situation in East Timor, a former Portuguese colony which was annexed by Indonesia in 1976, could never be normalised until all of its political leaders were freed.
"If we want a real settlement, that must be the result of the agreement between the Indonesian government and the leadership of East Timor," he added.
Murdiono however reiterated Jakarta's stand that Gusmao was in jail for criminal offences.

"I think our stand is clear. Xanana was sentenced not because of his political beliefs. Nobody can be sentenced because of political beliefs. People can be sentenced only for criminal acts," Murdiono said.
Diplomats in Jakarta said the situation seemed to be running out of Indonesia's control.

"I think the developments are surprising the Indonesians," said one. "They were probably thinking it would be well-scripted but they can't stop the process now. They would only look bad if they tried."

During Wednesday's comments, Mandela emphasised he was working within a framework forged by the United Nations, which has been brokering the so far unsuccessful talks between Portugal and Indonesia on the future of East Timor.
"We are not looking for any benefits. We are members of... an organisation which is committed to the promotion of peace," Mandela said.
During a recent visit to Indonesia, Mandela secured the temporary release of Gusmao from Jakarta's notorious Cipinang jail and dined with him at the government guest house next to Suharto's palace.
Mandela said he was struck during the meeting by what he called Gusmao's "outstanding qualities", his commitment and principles.
He briefly met Gusmao's spokesman in exile, Nobel peace laureate Jose Ramos-Horta, in Pretoria after his return from Indonesia and on Wednesday briefed the Portuguese leader on these discussions.
Portugal backs the resistance movement's call for the people of East Timor, where a small guerrilla force is still active, to be allowed to vote on their future.
"The role of Portugal is pivotal. There can be no settlement without the involvement of Portugal," Mandela said.
Mandela said South Africa's initiatives would be guided by the Timor leadership, both within and outside the territory, and added he hoped for a summit between them in the future.
